True Statement: In majority of dicotyledonous plants, the direct elongation of the radicle leads to the formation of primary root which grows inside the soil — forming the tap root system (e.g., mustard).
False 1: In majority of monocotyledonous plants, the direct elongation of the radicle leads to the formation of primary root and tap root system.
False 2: In majority of dicotyledonous plants, the primary root is short lived and replaced by a fibrous root system.

True Statement: In monocotyledonous plants, the primary root is short lived and is replaced by a large number of roots that originate from the base of the stem — constituting the fibrous root system (e.g., wheat).
False 1: In dicotyledonous plants, the primary root is short lived and replaced by fibrous roots from the base of the stem.
False 2: In monocotyledonous plants, the primary root persists throughout the life of the plant forming the tap root system.

True Statement: In some plants like grass, Monstera and the banyan tree, roots arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle and are called adventitious roots.
False 1: In some plants like grass, Monstera and the banyan tree, roots arise from the radicle and are called adventitious roots.
False 2: In mustard and wheat, roots arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle and are called adventitious roots.

True Statement: The main functions of the root system are absorption of water and minerals, providing anchorage, storing reserve food material and synthesis of plant growth regulators.
False 1: The main function of the root system is photosynthesis and synthesis of food.
False 2: The main functions of the stem are absorption of water and minerals, providing anchorage and storing reserve food.

True Statement: The root is covered at the apex by a thimble-like structure called the root cap which protects the tender apex as it makes its way through the soil.
False 1: The root is covered at the apex by root hairs which protect the tender apex as it makes its way through the soil.
False 2: The root is covered at the base by the root cap which protects the tender apex.

True Statement: A few millimetres above the root cap is the region of meristematic activity; cells here are very small, thin-walled with dense protoplasm and divide repeatedly.
False 1: The cells of the meristematic region are large, thick-walled and divide infrequently.
False 2: The region of meristematic activity is located a few millimetres below the root cap.

True Statement: The cells proximal to the meristematic region undergo rapid elongation and enlargement and are responsible for the growth of the root in length — this region is called the region of elongation.
False 1: The cells of the meristematic region undergo rapid elongation and enlargement, responsible for root growth in length.
False 2: The region of elongation is located proximal to the region of maturation, not to the meristematic region.

True Statement: From the region of maturation, some epidermal cells form very fine, thread-like structures called root hairs which absorb water and minerals from the soil.
False 1: Root hairs form from the meristematic region, not from the region of maturation.
False 2: Root hairs, formed from the region of maturation, provide anchorage to the plant rather than absorbing water.

True Statement: The stem is the ascending part of the axis bearing branches, leaves, flowers and fruits and develops from the plumule of the embryo.
False 1: The stem develops from the radicle of the embryo of a germinating seed.
False 2: The root is the ascending part of the axis bearing branches, leaves, flowers and fruits.

True Statement: The region of the stem where leaves are born are called nodes while internodes are the portions between two nodes.
False 1: The region where leaves are born are called internodes while nodes are the portions between two leaf-bearing regions.
False 2: The region where leaves are born are called rachis while internodes are the portions between two nodes.

True Statement: The main function of the stem is spreading out branches bearing leaves, flowers and fruits, and conducting water, minerals and photosynthates.
False 1: The main function of the stem is absorption of water and minerals from the soil.
False 2: The main function of the root is conducting water, minerals and photosynthates to all parts.

True Statement: The leaf is a lateral, generally flattened structure borne on the stem; it develops at the node and bears a bud in its axil.
False 1: The leaf develops at the internode and bears a bud at the node.
False 2: The leaf bears a bud in the axil of leaflets, not in the axil of the petiole.

True Statement: Leaves are the most important vegetative organs for photosynthesis.
False 1: Stems are the most important vegetative organs for photosynthesis.
False 2: Roots are the most important vegetative organs for photosynthesis.

True Statement: A typical leaf consists of three main parts: leaf base, petiole and lamina.
False 1: A typical leaf consists of three main parts: leaf base, rachis and lamina.
False 2: A typical leaf consists of two main parts: petiole and lamina, without a distinct leaf base.

True Statement: In monocotyledons, the leaf base expands into a sheath covering the stem partially or wholly.
False 1: In dicotyledons, the leaf base expands into a sheath covering the stem partially or wholly.
False 2: In monocotyledons, the petiole (not the leaf base) expands into a sheath covering the stem.

True Statement: In some leguminous plants, the leaf base may become swollen, which is called the pulvinus.
False 1: In some monocotyledonous plants, the leaf base may become swollen, called the pulvinus.
False 2: In some leguminous plants, the petiole (not the leaf base) may become swollen, called the pulvinus.

True Statement: The middle prominent vein is known as the midrib; veins provide rigidity to the leaf blade and act as channels of transport.
False 1: The middle prominent vein is known as the rachis.
False 2: Veins provide flexibility (not rigidity) to the leaf blade.

True Statement: When veinlets form a network, the venation is termed reticulate; when veins run parallel, it is termed parallel.
False 1: When veins run parallel to each other, the venation is termed reticulate.
False 2: When veinlets form a network, the venation is termed parallel.

True Statement: Leaves of dicotyledonous plants generally possess reticulate venation, while parallel venation is the characteristic of most monocotyledons.
False 1: Leaves of dicotyledonous plants generally possess parallel venation, while reticulate venation is characteristic of most monocotyledons.
False 2: Both dicotyledons and monocotyledons show reticulate venation.

True Statement: A leaf is said to be simple when its lamina is entire or when incised, the incisions do not touch the midrib.
False 1: A leaf is said to be simple when incisions of the lamina reach up to the midrib.
False 2: A leaf is said to be compound when its lamina is entire or when incisions do not reach the midrib.

True Statement: When the incisions of the lamina reach up to the midrib breaking it into leaflets, the leaf is called compound.
False 1: When incisions do not touch the midrib, the leaf is called compound.
False 2: A leaf with a continuous undivided lamina is called compound.

True Statement: A bud is present in the axil of the petiole in both simple and compound leaves, but not in the axil of leaflets of compound leaves.
False 1: A bud is present in the axil of leaflets in compound leaves, not in the axil of the petiole.
False 2: Buds are absent in both simple and compound leaves.

True Statement: In a pinnately compound leaf, a number of leaflets are present on a common axis called the rachis — as in neem.
False 1: In a palmately compound leaf, leaflets are present on a common axis called the rachis.
False 2: In a pinnately compound leaf, leaflets are attached at a common point at the tip of the petiole, as in neem.

True Statement: In palmately compound leaves, leaflets are attached at a common point, i.e., at the tip of the petiole — as in silk cotton.
False 1: In pinnately compound leaves, leaflets are attached at a common point at the tip of petiole.
False 2: In palmately compound leaves, leaflets are present on a common axis (rachis), as in silk cotton.

True Statement: Phyllotaxy is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch.
False 1: Phyllotaxy is the pattern of arrangement of flowers on the floral axis.
False 2: Venation is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch.

True Statement: In alternate phyllotaxy, a single leaf arises at each node in alternate manner — as in china rose, mustard and sunflower.
False 1: In opposite phyllotaxy, a single leaf arises at each node in alternate manner.
False 2: In alternate phyllotaxy, a single leaf arises at each node, as in Calotropis and guava.

True Statement: In opposite phyllotaxy, a pair of leaves arise at each node and lie opposite to each other — as in Calotropis and guava.
False 1: In alternate phyllotaxy, a pair of leaves arise at each node and lie opposite to each other.
False 2: In opposite phyllotaxy, a pair of leaves arise at each node, as in china rose and sunflower.

True Statement: In whorled phyllotaxy, more than two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl — as in Alstonia.
False 1: In whorled phyllotaxy, exactly two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl.
False 2: In whorled phyllotaxy, more than two leaves arise at a node, as in Calotropis.

True Statement: A flower is a modified shoot wherein the shoot apical meristem changes to floral meristem.
False 1: A flower is a modified root wherein the root apical meristem changes to floral meristem.
False 2: A flower is not a modified shoot; it is a distinct structure independent of the vegetative shoot.

True Statement: The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is termed inflorescence.
False 1: The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is termed phyllotaxy.
False 2: The arrangement of leaves on the stem is termed inflorescence.

True Statement: In racemose inflorescence, the main axis continues to grow and the flowers are borne laterally in an acropetal succession.
False 1: In cymose inflorescence, the main axis continues to grow and flowers are borne in acropetal succession.
False 2: In racemose inflorescence, the main axis terminates in a flower and flowers are borne in basipetal order.

True Statement: In cymose inflorescence, the main axis terminates in a flower (limited in growth) and flowers are borne in basipetal order.
False 1: In racemose inflorescence, the main axis terminates in a flower and flowers are borne in basipetal order.
False 2: In cymose inflorescence, the main axis continues to grow and flowers are borne in acropetal order.

True Statement: The flower is the reproductive unit in the angiosperms and is meant for sexual reproduction.
False 1: The fruit is the reproductive unit in angiosperms.
False 2: The flower is the vegetative unit in angiosperms, not meant for sexual reproduction.

True Statement: A typical flower has four whorls arranged on the thalamus: calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
False 1: A typical flower has three whorls: calyx, corolla and androecium (gynoecium is the pistil, not a whorl).
False 2: A typical flower has four whorls: calyx, corolla, androecium and perianth.

True Statement: Calyx and corolla are accessory organs, while androecium and gynoecium are reproductive organs.
False 1: Calyx and corolla are reproductive organs, while androecium and gynoecium are accessory organs.
False 2: Androecium and corolla are accessory organs, while calyx and gynoecium are reproductive organs.

True Statement: In flowers like lily, the calyx and corolla are not distinct and are termed perianth.
False 1: In flowers like rose, the calyx and corolla are not distinct and are termed perianth.
False 2: In lily, the calyx and corolla are very distinct; perianth applies only to monocot herbs.

True Statement: When a flower has both androecium and gynoecium, it is bisexual; a flower having only stamens or only carpels is unisexual.
False 1: When a flower has both androecium and gynoecium, it is unisexual.
False 2: A flower having only stamens is called bisexual and having only carpels makes it unisexual.

True Statement: When a flower can be divided into two equal radial halves in any radial plane, it is actinomorphic — e.g., mustard, datura, chilli.
False 1: When a flower can be divided into two similar halves only in one vertical plane, it is actinomorphic.
False 2: When a flower can be divided into equal radial halves in any radial plane, it is actinomorphic — e.g., pea, gulmohur, bean.

True Statement: When a flower can be divided into two similar halves only in one particular vertical plane, it is zygomorphic — e.g., pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia.
False 1: When a flower can be divided into equal halves in any radial plane, it is zygomorphic.
False 2: When a flower can be divided into two similar halves in only one plane, it is zygomorphic — e.g., mustard, datura, chilli.

True Statement: A flower is asymmetric (irregular) if it cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane passing through the centre — as in canna.
False 1: A flower is actinomorphic if it cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane.
False 2: A flower is asymmetric if it cannot be divided into similar halves — as in mustard.

True Statement: In hypogynous flowers, the gynoecium occupies the highest position, other parts are below it, and the ovary is superior — e.g., mustard, china rose, brinjal.
False 1: In epigynous flowers, the gynoecium occupies the highest position and the ovary is superior.
False 2: In hypogynous flowers the ovary is superior — e.g., plum, rose and peach.

True Statement: In perigynous flowers, gynoecium is in the centre and other parts are on the rim at the same level; the ovary is half inferior — e.g., plum, rose, peach.
False 1: In epigynous flowers, gynoecium is in the centre and other parts at the same level; the ovary is half inferior.
False 2: In perigynous flowers the ovary is half inferior — e.g., mustard, china rose and brinjal.

True Statement: In epigynous flowers, the thalamus grows upward enclosing the ovary completely and fusing with it; the ovary is inferior — e.g., guava, cucumber, ray florets of sunflower.
False 1: In hypogynous flowers, the thalamus encloses the ovary completely and the ovary is inferior.
False 2: In epigynous flowers the ovary is inferior — e.g., plum, rose and peach.

True Statement: The calyx is the outermost whorl of the flower; its members are called sepals; they are generally green and leaf-like and protect the flower in the bud stage.
False 1: The corolla is the outermost whorl of the flower; its members are called sepals.
False 2: The calyx is the innermost whorl of the flower; its members are called petals.

True Statement: The calyx may be gamosepalous (sepals united) or polysepalous (sepals free).
False 1: Gamosepalous means sepals are free and polysepalous means sepals are united.
False 2: The corolla may be gamosepalous (sepals united) or polysepalous (sepals free).

True Statement: Petals are usually brightly coloured to attract insects for pollination.
False 1: Sepals are usually brightly coloured to attract insects for pollination.
False 2: Petals are usually brightly coloured to protect the flower in the bud stage.

True Statement: Corolla may be gamopetalous (petals united) or polypetalous (petals free).
False 1: Gamopetalous means petals are free and polypetalous means petals are united.
False 2: Calyx may be gamopetalous (petals united) or polypetalous (petals free).

True Statement: In valvate aestivation, sepals or petals just touch one another at the margin without overlapping — as in Calotropis.
False 1: In twisted aestivation, sepals or petals just touch one another at the margin without overlapping.
False 2: In valvate aestivation, sepals or petals just touch without overlapping, as in china rose.

True Statement: In twisted aestivation, one margin of the appendage overlaps the next one and so on — as in china rose, lady's finger and cotton.
False 1: In imbricate aestivation, one margin of the appendage overlaps the next one and so on.
False 2: In twisted aestivation, one margin overlaps the next, as in Cassia and gulmohur.

True Statement: In imbricate aestivation, margins of sepals or petals overlap one another but not in any particular direction — as in Cassia and gulmohur.
False 1: In twisted aestivation, margins overlap without any particular direction, as in Cassia.
False 2: In imbricate aestivation, margins overlap without particular direction, as in china rose and cotton.

True Statement: In vexillary (papilionaceous) aestivation, the largest petal (standard) overlaps two lateral petals (wings) which in turn overlap the two smallest anterior petals (keel) — as in pea and bean.
False 1: In imbricate aestivation, the largest petal (standard) overlaps two lateral petals (wings) and the keel, as in pea and bean.
False 2: In vexillary aestivation, the two smallest petals (keel) overlap the wings which overlap the standard.

True Statement: Each stamen consists of a stalk (filament) and an anther; each anther is usually bilobed and each lobe has two chambers called pollen-sacs.
False 1: Each anther is usually unilobed and has a single pollen-sac per anther.
False 2: Each carpel consists of a filament and an anther; each anther is bilobed with two pollen-sacs.

True Statement: A sterile stamen is called staminode.
False 1: A sterile carpel is called staminode.
False 2: A fertile stamen is called staminode.

True Statement: When stamens are attached to the petals, they are epipetalous (e.g., brinjal) or epiphyllous when attached to the perianth (e.g., lily).
False 1: Epiphyllous means stamens attached to petals; epipetalous means attached to perianth.
False 2: Stamens are epipetalous in lily and epiphyllous in brinjal.

True Statement: Stamens united into one bundle are monoadelphous (china rose), two bundles diadelphous (pea), more than two bundles polyadelphous (citrus).
False 1: Stamens united into two bundles are monoadelphous and into one bundle are diadelphous.
False 2: Monoadelphous stamens are found in pea and diadelphous in china rose.

True Statement: Gynoecium is the female reproductive part of the flower made up of one or more carpels; a carpel consists of three parts: stigma, style and ovary.
False 1: Androecium is the female reproductive part of the flower made up of carpels.
False 2: A carpel consists of three parts: filament, anther and ovary.

True Statement: The stigma is usually at the tip of the style and is the receptive surface for pollen grains.
False 1: The style is at the tip of the stigma and is the receptive surface for pollen grains.
False 2: The stigma is at the base of the style and is the receptive surface for pollen grains.

True Statement: When more than one carpel is present and they are free, they are called apocarpous (e.g., lotus and rose); when fused, syncarpous (e.g., mustard and tomato).
False 1: Apocarpous means carpels are fused and syncarpous means carpels are free.
False 2: Apocarpous carpels are found in mustard and tomato; syncarpous in lotus and rose.

True Statement: After fertilisation, the ovules develop into seeds and the ovary matures into a fruit.
False 1: After fertilisation, the ovules develop into fruits and the ovary matures into seeds.
False 2: After fertilisation, the ovules develop into seeds and the thalamus matures into a fruit.

True Statement: In marginal placentation, the placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture and ovules are borne on this ridge in two rows — as in pea.
False 1: In axile placentation, the placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture and ovules are borne in two rows.
False 2: In marginal placentation, ovules are borne on a ridge in two rows, as in tomato and lemon.

True Statement: In axile placentation, ovules are attached to axial placenta in a multilocular ovary — as in china rose, tomato and lemon.
False 1: In marginal placentation, ovules are attached to axial placenta in a multilocular ovary.
False 2: In axile placentation, ovules attach to axial placenta as in pea and Argemone.

True Statement: In parietal placentation, ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary; the ovary is one-chambered but becomes two-chambered due to a false septum — as in mustard and Argemone.
False 1: In axile placentation, the ovary is one-chambered but becomes two-chambered due to a false septum.
False 2: In parietal placentation, the ovary is initially one-chambered, as in pea and china rose.

True Statement: In free central placentation, ovules are borne on a central axis and septa are absent — as in Dianthus and Primrose.
False 1: In basal placentation, ovules are borne on a central axis and septa are absent.
False 2: In free central placentation, ovules are on a central axis, as in sunflower and marigold.

True Statement: In basal placentation, the placenta develops at the base of the ovary and a single ovule is attached to it — as in sunflower and marigold.
False 1: In free central placentation, placenta develops at the base of the ovary and a single ovule is attached.
False 2: In basal placentation, a single ovule attaches at the base, as in Dianthus and Primrose.

True Statement: The fruit is a mature or ripened ovary, developed after fertilisation.
False 1: The seed is a mature or ripened ovary, developed after fertilisation.
False 2: The fruit is a mature or ripened ovule, developed after fertilisation.

True Statement: If a fruit is formed without fertilisation of the ovary, it is called a parthenocarpic fruit.
False 1: A fruit formed after fertilisation of the ovary is called a parthenocarpic fruit.
False 2: If a seed is formed without fertilisation, it is called a parthenocarpic seed.

True Statement: When pericarp is thick and fleshy, it is differentiated into the outer epicarp, the middle mesocarp and the inner endocarp.
False 1: The outer layer of pericarp is endocarp, the middle is mesocarp and the inner is epicarp.
False 2: The thick fleshy pericarp has two layers: epicarp and mesocarp only; there is no endocarp.

True Statement: In mango and coconut, the fruit is known as a drupe — developing from monocarpellary superior ovaries and one-seeded.
False 1: In mango and coconut, the fruit is known as a berry — one-seeded from monocarpellary ovaries.
False 2: Drupes are many-seeded fruits developing from multicarpellary ovaries.

True Statement: In mango, the pericarp is differentiated into an outer thin epicarp, a middle fleshy edible mesocarp and an inner stony hard endocarp.
False 1: In mango, the middle mesocarp is stony and the inner endocarp is fleshy and edible.
False 2: In coconut, the pericarp is differentiated into outer thin epicarp, middle fleshy edible mesocarp and inner stony endocarp.

True Statement: In coconut, the mesocarp is fibrous.
False 1: In coconut, the mesocarp is fleshy and edible.
False 2: In mango, the mesocarp is fibrous.

True Statement: A seed is made up of a seed coat and an embryo; the embryo consists of a radicle, an embryonal axis and one (monocots) or two cotyledons (dicots).
False 1: A seed has two cotyledons in monocots (e.g., wheat, maize) and one in dicots (e.g., gram, pea).
False 2: A seed is made up of a pericarp and an embryo; the seed coat is part of the fruit.

True Statement: The seed coat has two layers: the outer testa and the inner tegmen.
False 1: The seed coat has two layers: the outer tegmen and the inner testa.
False 2: The seed coat has three layers: testa, tegmen and aleurone layer.

True Statement: The hilum is a scar on the seed coat through which the developing seed was attached to the fruit.
False 1: The micropyle is a scar on the seed coat through which the developing seed was attached to the fruit.
False 2: The hilum is a scar on the seed coat through which water enters the seed during germination.

True Statement: Above the hilum is a small pore called the micropyle.
False 1: Above the hilum is a small pore called the testa.
False 2: Below the hilum is a small pore called the micropyle.

True Statement: In some seeds such as castor, the endosperm formed by double fertilisation is a food-storing tissue — such seeds are endospermic.
False 1: In seeds such as bean, gram and pea, the endosperm is a food-storing tissue — these are endospermic.
False 2: In castor, endosperm is absent and food is stored entirely in the cotyledons.

True Statement: In plants such as bean, gram and pea, the endosperm is not present in mature seeds — called non-endospermous.
False 1: In castor, endosperm is not present in mature seeds — called non-endospermous.
False 2: Bean, gram and pea seeds are endospermic because they store food in the endosperm.

True Statement: Generally monocotyledonous seeds are endospermic, but some as in orchids are non-endospermic.
False 1: Generally monocotyledonous seeds are non-endospermic.
False 2: Generally dicotyledonous seeds are endospermic; monocotyledonous seeds are mostly non-endospermic.

True Statement: In maize, the outer covering of endosperm separates the embryo by a proteinous layer called the aleurone layer.
False 1: In maize, the aleurone layer is located inside the endosperm, not between the endosperm and embryo.
False 2: In maize, food is stored in the cotyledon (scutellum) and the endosperm is reduced.

True Statement: The single large shield-shaped cotyledon in the monocot seed is known as scutellum.
False 1: The single large shield-shaped cotyledon in the monocot seed is known as aleurone layer.
False 2: The scutellum is the proteinous outer layer of the endosperm in monocot seeds.

True Statement: The plumule is enclosed in a sheath called coleoptile; the radicle is enclosed in a sheath called coleorhiza.
False 1: The plumule is enclosed in the coleorhiza and the radicle is enclosed in the coleoptile.
False 2: The plumule is enclosed in a sheath called coleorhiza and the radicle in the coleoptile.

True Statement: Solanaceae is a large family commonly called the 'potato family', widely distributed in tropics, subtropics and temperate zones.
False 1: Solanaceae is commonly called the 'tomato family'.
False 2: Solanaceae is found only in tropical and subtropical regions.

True Statement: Solanaceae inflorescence is solitary axillary or cymose, as in Solanum.
False 1: Solanaceae inflorescence is racemose, as in Solanum.
False 2: Solanaceae inflorescence is always solitary and never cymose.

True Statement: Solanaceae flowers are bisexual and actinomorphic.
False 1: Solanaceae flowers are bisexual and zygomorphic.
False 2: Solanaceae flowers are unisexual and actinomorphic.

True Statement: In Solanaceae, calyx has five sepals that are united (gamosepalous), persistent and show valvate aestivation.
False 1: In Solanaceae, calyx has five free (polysepalous) sepals that are deciduous.
False 2: In Solanaceae, corolla has five sepals that are united with valvate aestivation.

True Statement: In Solanaceae, corolla has five united petals (gamopetalous) with valvate aestivation.
False 1: In Solanaceae, corolla has five free petals (polypetalous).
False 2: In Solanaceae, calyx has five united petals with valvate aestivation.

True Statement: In Solanaceae, androecium has five stamens that are epipetalous.
False 1: In Solanaceae, androecium has five stamens that are free (not attached to petals).
False 2: In Solanaceae, androecium has five stamens that are epiphyllous (attached to perianth).

True Statement: In Solanaceae, gynoecium is bicarpellary syncarpous with superior ovary, bilocular with axile placentation.
False 1: In Solanaceae, the ovary is inferior (not superior).
False 2: In Solanaceae, the ovary is unilocular with parietal placentation.

True Statement: In Solanaceae, fruits are berry or capsule; seeds are many and endospermous.
False 1: In Solanaceae, fruits are drupe or nut; seeds are few and non-endospermous.
False 2: In Solanaceae, seeds are few and non-endospermous (exalbuminous).

True Statement: Plants of Solanaceae are sources of food (tomato, brinjal, potato), spice (chilli), medicine (belladonna, ashwagandha) and fumigatory (tobacco).
False 1: Plants of Solanaceae are sources of food (tomato, brinjal, potato) and spice (black pepper), medicine and fumigatory.
False 2: Tobacco belongs to family Fabaceae, not Solanaceae.
